assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, built on Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and realised with Sr and Yb, reached fractional uncertainties near 1e-18 and now define the frontier of timekeeping. They are a clear case of a new measurement capability that opens other work: relativistic geodesy, tests of fundamental constants and dark-matter searches, and the redefinition of the second. This is the kind of work I value most, because precision is what limits knowledge.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and made the first demonstrations. Jun Ye's JILA group brought the clock to its present performance and ran the key comparisons. Two laureates give a clean and defensible configuration. Other groups (for example Lemonde, Ludlow) made contributions, but they are secondary to these two as far as I know.
assessment.maturity: Mature. Many independent labs reproduce the 1e-18 level and clock comparisons run across institutions. Timing is good, and the 2005 comb prize leaves room for the clock itself.
uncertainties: Whether the committee would want the lattice clock separated from earlier ion-clock and comb recognition.
I have not independently checked the credit for the magic-wavelength idea against that for the early Sr experiments.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Atom interferometry turned matter-wave coherence into a precision instrument for measuring gravity, rotation and the fine-structure constant, and it is now used in gravitational-wave and equivalence-principle proposals. It is a method that opens new ways to observe nature, and it is original. The experimental depth is high.
assessment.attribution: Pritchard's group made early atom interferometers with gratings, Bordé gave the Ramsey-Bordé theory, and Kasevich with Chu made the light-pulse interferometer and the gravimeters and gradiometers. Chu already holds a prize for cooling, which makes the Kasevich-Chu link a point to settle. A three-person set from the credited names is plausible, though the balance between Bordé and others is debatable.
assessment.maturity: Mature. Commercial gravimeters and many labs confirm it. The large-scale applications such as fundamental-physics tests are still under way, but the methods are established.
uncertainties: Fair weighting of Bordé's theoretical contribution against the experimental pioneers.
Whether a prize for the method overlaps too much with earlier laser-cooling recognition.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Squeezed light lets one beat the standard quantum limit in interferometry, and it is now routinely injected into LIGO, Virgo and GEO600 to improve their sensitivity. It links the theory of quantum noise to a real instrument and to a major discovery programme, and it is exactly the sort of measurement advance that I find convincing.
assessment.attribution: Caves provided the theoretical proposal for squeezed-vacuum interferometry. Kimble's group made the first experimental squeezed states and many later developments. Schnabel's group developed the practical, high-level squeezing and the GEO600 implementation. Mavalvala and others are also credited and the credit among many participants is crowded, so any three-person choice leaves out people.
assessment.maturity: Substantially mature since squeezing is in operating detectors. Credit is spread over decades, which complicates timing and selection.
uncertainties: Crowded attribution across four credited names and several unnamed contributors, such as Slusher and Walls.
Possible overlap with the 2017 gravitational-wave prize and the 2012 quantum optics prize.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED made superconducting qubits readable and controllable and is the base of the leading solid-state quantum computing platforms. It demonstrates strong coupling at the single-photon level on a chip, and it has opened both quantum information experiments and quantum sensing. The importance is high.
assessment.attribution: Blais, Girvin, Schoelkopf and collaborators wrote the 2004 proposal, and Wallraff with Schoelkopf demonstrated strong coupling. A configuration of Schoelkopf, Wallraff and Girvin fits, with Blais being the one left out. Credit among experiment and theory is mostly clear.
assessment.maturity: Mature in the basic physics, with many replications. The 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits makes timing sensitive, since the committee may want some distance before returning to the field.
uncertainties: Overlap with the recent recognition of superconducting circuits.
Blais is a strong theoretical co-originator who would be excluded by a three-person limit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical readout and coherent control of single nitrogen-vacancy centres gave a room-temperature solid-state qubit and a nanoscale sensor for magnetic fields, temperature and nuclear spins. It is a measurement technique with broad uptake in biology and materials. I find the sensing side to be the more durable contribution.
assessment.attribution: Wrachtrup's group first detected a single NV centre optically. Jelezko added coherent control and nuclear spin work, and Lukin contributed to sensing and quantum network proposals and experiments. Others such as Awschalom and Hanson are not credited here, so the proposed set is only one of several reasonable ones.
assessment.maturity: Reasonably mature as a method, with many groups confirming it. Real-world sensing impact is still growing, and so it may be a little early for the applications.
uncertainties: Absence of other major NV groups in the credited names.
Whether the sensing or the qubit side is the main prize-worthy contribution.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cavity optomechanics brought mechanical oscillators to the quantum ground state and enabled squeezed and entangled motion and quantum-limited displacement sensing. These are well-controlled experiments with clear measured numbers, and the methods apply to sensing and transduction. The foundational insight is clear.
assessment.attribution: Kippenberg and Aspelmeyer drove the cavity side of the field, including sideband cooling and the reviews. Cleland, with O'Connell and Martinis, demonstrated the mechanical ground state in an electrical circuit. Other leaders such as Painter and Harris are left out.
assessment.maturity: Moderately mature. Ground-state cooling and quantum control have been reproduced widely, though practical impact beyond the laboratory is still limited.
uncertainties: Credit is spread across the cavity and electromechanical routes, with Painter, Harris, Lehnert and others having close claims.
Practical use is not yet comparable to clocks or squeezed light.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices provide controllable quantum simulators for many-body physics, including the superfluid to Mott insulator transition and single-site imaging. They open the way to new observations of strongly correlated matter. The importance is high, though the concrete discoveries are varied.
assessment.attribution: Zoller and Jaksch gave the theory proposal, Greiner and Bloch carried out the Mott insulator experiment, and Esslinger demonstrated fermionic Hubbard physics. I pick three of the four-plus names, and this leaves out Greiner, whose role was decisive in the first experiment.
assessment.maturity: Mature as a field and widely reproduced. A prize for the whole would be broad, and the 2001 condensate prize and the 2012 prize on single quantum systems lie close by.
uncertainties: Whether the discovery is a single clear one or a broad programme.
Choosing three from an obviously larger group is difficult, and Greiner's role could argue for his inclusion.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Ti:sapphire laser and Kerr-lens mode locking became the workhorse of ultrafast science, including frequency combs, attosecond physics and spectroscopy. I know from the laser spectroscopy tradition how much work rests on it. The impact beyond physics is very large, and it is a clear enabling invention.
assessment.attribution: Moulton invented the Ti:sapphire gain medium, and Sibbett's group demonstrated Kerr-lens mode locking, with Spence and Keller among others close behind. The two-person set is workable, though the Kerr-lens credit is a bit spread.
assessment.maturity: Very mature, as the technology is decades old. The long delay and the 2018 and 2023 recognitions of related work make this lower in priority.
uncertainties: Distribution of credit for Kerr-lens mode locking among Sibbett, Spence, Keller and others.
Possible view that the invention has already been recognised indirectly through combs, chirped pulses and attosecond physics.
